--- title: "S0-02 notebook — R" subtitle: "Units, scaling and allometry" execute: freeze: auto --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) library(ggplot2) theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 11)) truth <- read.csv("../../cases/case-sm/data/ozanib_individual_truth.csv") MW <- 465; FU <- 0.08 # g/mol, fraction unbound ``` ::: ## 1. Conversions, written once ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ng_ml_to_nM <- function(x, mw) x / mw * 1000 nM_to_ng_ml <- function(x, mw) x * mw / 1000 L_per_h_to_mL_min <- function(x) x * 1000 / 60 conc <- c(`steady-state trough` = 51.9, `steady-state peak` = 560.7) for (nm in names(conc)) { cat(sprintf("%-22s %7.1f ng/mL = %7.1f nM total = %6.1f nM free\n", nm, conc[[nm]], ng_ml_to_nM(conc[[nm]], MW), ng_ml_to_nM(conc[[nm]] * FU, MW))) } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` steady-state trough 51.9 ng/mL = 111.6 nM total = 8.9 nM free steady-state peak 560.7 ng/mL = 1205.8 nM total = 96.5 nM free ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("\nCL/F = 12 L/h = %.0f mL/min = %.3f L/h/kg at 70 kg\n", L_per_h_to_mL_min(12), 12 / 70)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` CL/F = 12 L/h = 200 mL/min = 0.171 L/h/kg at 70 kg ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("hepatic blood flow ~ 90 L/h (%.0f mL/min)\n", L_per_h_to_mL_min(90))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` hepatic blood flow ~ 90 L/h (1500 mL/min) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("GFR ~ 7.5 L/h (%.0f mL/min)\n", L_per_h_to_mL_min(7.5))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` GFR ~ 7.5 L/h (125 mL/min) ``` ::: ::: An *in vitro* IC~50~ of 200 nM sits **above** the free peak of 96 nM. Compare against total concentrations and you would conclude the opposite. ## 2. Recovering the allometric exponent — from the truth itself ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} clean <- truth |> filter(DDI == 0) fit <- lm(log(CL) ~ log(WT / 70), data = clean) ci <- confint(fit)["log(WT/70)", ] cat(sprintf("n = %d subjects, weight range %.0f-%.0f kg\n", nrow(clean), min(clean$WT), max(clean$WT))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` n = 46 subjects, weight range 46-118 kg ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("exponent on CL : %.3f (truth 0.75) 95%% CI %.2f to %.2f\n", coef(fit)[2], ci[1], ci[2])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` exponent on CL : 0.934 (truth 0.75) 95% CI 0.56 to 1.31 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("CL at 70 kg : %.2f L/h (truth 12.0)\n", exp(coef(fit)[1]))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` CL at 70 kg : 11.57 L/h (truth 12.0) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} fit_v <- lm(log(VC) ~ log(WT / 70), data = clean) cat(sprintf("exponent on Vc : %.3f (truth 1.00) Vc at 70 kg %.1f L (truth 60.0)\n", coef(fit_v)[2], exp(coef(fit_v)[1]))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` exponent on Vc : 1.008 (truth 1.00) Vc at 70 kg 58.1 L (truth 60.0) ``` ::: ::: The point estimate for clearance misses 0.75 substantially, and the interval is wide enough to contain both 0.75 and 1.0 — on **error-free** individual parameters. That is the argument for fixing the exponents rather than estimating them. ## 3. Confounding: what an omitted covariate does ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_all <- lm(log(CL) ~ log(WT / 70), data = truth) cat(sprintf("exponent ignoring the DDI covariate : %.3f (truth 0.75)\n", coef(fit_all)[2])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` exponent ignoring the DDI covariate : 1.145 (truth 0.75) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("CL at 70 kg : %.2f L/h (truth 12.0)\n", exp(coef(fit_all)[1]))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` CL at 70 kg : 9.82 L/h (truth 12.0) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} fit_adj <- lm(log(CL) ~ log(WT / 70) + factor(DDI), data = truth) cat(sprintf("exponent WITH the DDI covariate : %.3f\n", coef(fit_adj)[2])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` exponent WITH the DDI covariate : 0.915 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("inhibitor effect on CL : x%.2f (truth 0.45)\n", exp(coef(fit_adj)[3]))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` inhibitor effect on CL : x0.50 (truth 0.45) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} truth |> mutate(arm = ifelse(DDI == 1, "strong CYP3A4 inhibitor", "no inhibitor")) |> ggplot(aes(WT, CL, shape = arm, colour = arm)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.85) + stat_function(fun = function(w) 12 * (w / 70)^0.75, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.4) + stat_function(fun = function(w) 12 * 0.45 * (w / 70)^0.75, colour = "black", linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.4) + scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() + labs(x = "Weight (kg)", y = "True CL/F (L/h)", colour = NULL, shape = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "top") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](notebook-r_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The inhibitor-treated subjects sit on a lower line. Fit one line through both clouds and the slope tilts. **An omitted covariate does not vanish; it redistributes into the covariates you kept.** ## 4. Flat versus weight-based dosing Because the model is linear, `AUC(tau,ss) = D / CL` exactly — no simulation needed. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cv_pct <- function(x) 100 * sd(x) / mean(x) auc_flat <- 50 * 1000 / truth$CL auc_wb <- (0.7 * truth$WT) * 1000 / truth$CL data.frame( strategy = c("flat 50 mg", "weight-based 0.7 mg/kg"), mean_AUC = c(mean(auc_flat), mean(auc_wb)), CV_pct = c(cv_pct(auc_flat), cv_pct(auc_wb)), p5 = c(quantile(auc_flat, .05), quantile(auc_wb, .05)), p95 = c(quantile(auc_flat, .95), quantile(auc_wb, .95)), spread = c(quantile(auc_flat, .95) / quantile(auc_flat, .05), quantile(auc_wb, .95) / quantile(auc_wb, .05)) ) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|strategy | mean_AUC| CV_pct| p5| p95| spread| |:----------------------|--------:|------:|------:|-------:|------:| |flat 50 mg | 5537.2| 51.5| 2570.9| 10993.2| 4.3| |weight-based 0.7 mg/kg | 5394.7| 44.1| 3052.9| 10566.3| 3.5|
::: ::: Weight-based dosing narrows the distribution by about 7 percentage points of CV. Whether that is worth the operational cost is a **therapeutic-index** question, not a statistical one. ## 5. How much of the variability is weight at all? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} r2 <- summary(lm(log(CL) ~ log(WT), data = clean))$r.squared cat(sprintf("R^2 of log(WT) on log(CL), inhibitor-free subjects: %.3f\n", r2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` R^2 of log(WT) on log(CL), inhibitor-free subjects: 0.361 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} cat(sprintf("-> weight explains about %.0f%% of between-subject variation in clearance\n", 100 * r2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` -> weight explains about 36% of between-subject variation in clearance ``` ::: ::: Usually smaller than people expect, and the honest answer to "should we dose per kilogram?" ## What to try next 1. Repeat section 2 on subjects between 60 and 85 kg. How wide does the interval get? 2. Compare `fit_adj` to `fit_all` — that is covariate modeling in one line. 3. Find the mg/kg dose matching the median AUC of flat 50 mg, then compare the fraction above a hypothetical toxicity threshold of 8000 ng·h/mL under each.
